title: Memoization: memo, useMemo & useCallback
objectives: Explain how memo() skips a re-render only when every prop is shallow-equal by Object.is
Predict whether a memo child re-renders when its parent passes inline objects or functions
Choose between useMemo (cache a value) and useCallback (cache a function), with the right deps
Fix a memo child's needless re-renders by giving its callback prop a stable identity with useCallback
Spot memoization that buys nothing — cheap work that no memo child or Hook dependency consumes — and say what React Compiler changes

sources.title: React docs: Introduction to React Compiler

questions.prompt: What does wrapping a component in React.memo() actually do?

options.text: Skips re-rendering when its props are shallow-equal to the previous render's props
Caches the returned JSX forever, so the component never re-renders again
Memoizes the component's internal state so it survives unmounts
Deep-compares every prop, no matter how nested, before re-rendering

questions.explanation: memo does a shallow comparison of props (Object.is on each). If every prop is the same reference/value as last time, React reuses the previous render and skips the child. It does NOT deep-compare. A parent re-render alone won't usually re-render a memo child — changed props, or the child's own state or a context it reads, will. And it's a performance optimization, not a guarantee: react.dev says React may still re-render a memoized component, so your code must stay correct if it does.

questions.prompt: A memo() child still re-renders every time its parent updates. The most likely cause?

options.text: The parent passes a prop that is a freshly-created object/array/function each render, so shallow comparison fails
memo() is broken and needs a custom areEqual comparator to work at all
The child has its own useState, which disables memo
The parent renders too fast for memo to catch up

questions.explanation: An inline object literal, array, or arrow function gets a brand-new reference on every parent render. Object.is sees a different reference, so memo's shallow check fails and the child re-renders. Stabilize the identity with useMemo (values) or useCallback (functions).

questions.prompt: What's the difference between useMemo and useCallback?

options.text: useMemo caches the return value of a function; useCallback caches the function itself
Nothing — they're aliases for the same hook
useCallback is only for async functions; useMemo is for sync ones
useMemo runs side effects; useCallback runs computations

questions.explanation: useMemo(fn, deps) runs fn and caches its result, recomputing only when deps change. useCallback(fn, deps) caches the function reference itself. react.dev's simplified model: useCallback(fn, deps) behaves like useMemo(() => fn, deps). Reach for useMemo to skip an expensive computation or stabilize a derived object; useCallback to keep a function's identity stable for a memoized child or an effect dependency.

options.text: When the work is cheap and the result doesn't flow into a `memo` child or a Hook's dependency array
Never — memoizing always makes an app faster
When a child's props are primitives — `memo` can only compare objects
When the child is already wrapped in `memo` — then the parent's `useCallback` is redundant

questions.explanation: react.dev lists the cases where it pays: a calculation that's noticeably slow (around 1ms or more), a value or function passed to a `memo` child, or one used as a Hook dependency. Anywhere else it skips nothing. The comparison itself is cheap — react.dev calls over-memoizing no significant harm — but it costs readability and dependency arrays you must keep correct, and one always-new prop is enough to make it all dead weight. Primitives are where `memo` works best (`Object.is(3, 3)` is true), and `memo` without stable function props is exactly the case `useCallback` exists for.

questions.prompt: Your project turns on React Compiler (stable since v1.0, October 2025). What happens to the advice in this unit?

options.text: The compiler memoizes components, values and callbacks at build time, so most hand-written memoization becomes unnecessary; `useMemo`/`useCallback` remain escape hatches
Nothing changes — the compiler only strips dead code
`memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` stop working, so delete them all
Nothing to decide — every React 19 app already has the compiler turned on

questions.explanation: React Compiler analyses your components at build time and inserts the memoization you'd otherwise write by hand — react.dev's `memo` page says you typically don't need `React.memo` with it. For new code, react.dev recommends relying on it and keeping `useMemo`/`useCallback` as escape hatches (for example, to keep an Effect dependency stable). Existing memoization still works: leave it in place, or test before removing it, since removal can change the compiled output. It's a build plugin you add (Babel, Vite, Next.js and others; a few new-project templates, such as Expo SDK 54+, switch it on by default) and it works with React 17 and up — React 19 itself doesn't turn it on. In a project without it, everything in this unit applies as written.

prompts.prompt: Cache this expensive sort so it only recomputes when `items` changes.
prompts.explanation: useMemo(factory, deps) runs the factory and caches its result, re-running only when a dep changes (here, items). Between changes, `sorted` keeps the same reference — cheap for renders and stable if you pass it to a memo child.

prompts.prompt: Give this handler a stable identity so a memo() child doesn't re-render.
prompts.explanation: useCallback returns the same function reference across renders until a dep changes. Because the closure reads onSelect and id, both are deps — otherwise the callback would call a stale onSelect or the wrong id.

prompts.prompt: Wrap this child so it skips re-rendering when its props are shallow-equal.
prompts.explanation: memo(Component) returns a memoized component that shallow-compares its props and reuses the last render when they're unchanged. It only pays off if the props passed in are actually stable — pair it with useMemo/useCallback for object and function props.

code: const Child = memo(function Child({ onClick }: { onClick: () => void }) {
snippets.question: Without React Compiler: every time you click the count button, does the memo'd Child re-render (does "Child render" log again)?
snippets.answer: Yes — Child re-renders on every parent update
snippets.explanation: The onClick arrow is created fresh on every Parent render, so it's a new reference each time. memo's shallow prop check sees onClick change and re-renders Child — the memo buys nothing. Wrap the handler in useCallback(() => console.log('clicked'), []) to give it a stable identity; then Child renders once and skips the unrelated count updates. (With React Compiler enabled, the compiler would memoize that arrow for you and Child would stop re-rendering. In development, StrictMode calls each render twice, so every render logs twice — the yes/no answer is the same.)

code: const Child = memo(function Child({ style }: { style: object }) {
snippets.question: Without React Compiler, and with `style` wrapped in useMemo([]): does clicking the button re-render Child?
snippets.explanation: useMemo(() => ({ color: 'red' }), []) computes the object once and returns the same reference on every subsequent render. memo's shallow check sees an unchanged style prop and skips Child, so "Child render" logs only on the first mount. (Remove the useMemo and the inline object would break memo just like the inline callback above.)
